newsitem.title: USA: Democrats may seek veto of tax-cut bill - Gingrich.
newsitem.headline: Democrats may seek veto of tax-cut bill - Gingrich.

text.p: House Speaker Newt Gingrich said Saturday that Democrats might try to persuade President Clinton to veto a new tax-cutting measure approved this week by the House Ways and Means Committee.

While speaking to reporters in his home district, the Georgia Republican accused Democrats of wanting to turn the bill into a welfare measure by providing tax relief to the working poor and other low-income wage earners.

"I hope the president isn't planning to veto it. But I'm much more concerned since the vote the other night that there may well be an efffort on the part of the liberal Democrats to convince him to veto it," Gingrich said.

The bill won approval from the House committee early Friday despite unanimous opposition from member Democrats who said the measure favoured the rich and violated the bipartisan balanced-budget agreement by curtailing college tax breaks sought by the president.
The bill provides for $135 billion worth of tax cuts over five years, partially offset by $50 billion in new revenues from expanded taxes on airline tickets and the elimination of tax loopholes.

Among its main provisions, the measure would grant a tax credit of up to $500 for each child under 17 in families with incomes of up to $110,000, and reduce the top rate on capital gains for individuals from 28 percent to 20 percent.

Critics complain that the child tax credit would not be available to many low- and moderate-income families who receive the earned income tax credit. It also would limit credits for families claiming a credit for child-care expenses.
But Gingrich said that to do otherwise would be tantamount to providing welfare assistance.
"I'm for tax cuts going to people who pay taxes. They're for tax cuts going to people who don't pay taxes -- that's welfare," Gingrich said.
"And if that's part of their condition, we have a very, very big challenge, because we're not going to turn the tax-cut bill into a welfare bill."

Partisan wrangling over the measure already has spawned concerns that Congress could be on a collision course with the White House over how to parcel out reductions agreed under the balanced budget plan.
Clinton attacked the measure Friday by saying it would penalise the working poor and working mothers. But White House officials up to now have avoided explicit veto threats.
